title: COAR launches Retractions Task Force
content:
(photo credit: Salon/Getty Images)

Retractions usually take place on the journal website and by the publisher, without the information being conveyed to other platforms or infrastructures, such as a repository that hosts a copy of that article. In the 2012 paper, The Persistence of Error, Philip Davis found that most freely available copies of retracted biomedical papers outside the publisher’s site carried no notice of the retraction. As a result, those orphaned copies keep being read and cited and also critics can use unmarked retracted copies to argue that repositories spread discredited science or weaken quality control. With the explosive growth of fake and AI-generated papers and a significant increase in the number of article retractions each year, this is becoming an important issue for the repository community to address.

To support the adoption of good practices, COAR is launching a Task Force to develop recommended practices for managing retractions in repositories, with three main objectives:

  • Define the various terminologies related to retractions, corrections, removals, and expressions of concern)
